newsitem.title: UK: Britain's election campaign grows more vitriolic.
newsitem.headline: Britain's election campaign grows more vitriolic.

text.p: With an election less than a week away, the battle between Britain's ruling Conservatives and their Labour rivals is growing ever more vitriolic.
Prime Minister John Major, fighting a lost cause if opinion polls are right, turned in fury on Labour leader Tony Blair on Thursday, accusing him of lying and making "scurrilous" charges.
Blair had angered Major by saying the Conservatives would put taxes on food and abolish state pensions if it were re-elected on May 1 for an unprecedented fifth term of office.
"In plain terms they are lies...and I hope the Labour party will have the grace to withdraw them," Major said on a trip to an electronics factory in northern England.
But Blair refused to back down. "I do not withdraw a single iota of it," the Labour leader said on BBC television late on Thursday.
Media reports said Labour planned to return to the attack on the Conservatives' plans for pensions at its daily news conference on Friday morning.

The Conservatives recently proposed a scheme under which they said younger Britons could earn themselves a more comfortable old age by investing money which at present goes to the social welfare fund in private pension schemes.
But they insisted the scheme had a safety net which would guarantee a basic state pension even to those unlucky enough to invest in schemes that failed.
Labour said small print in the proposals showed the Conservatives planned to impose the scheme on older people as well.
Throughout the campaign Blair has repeatedly appealed for an end to personal attacks and more concentration on the issues at stake -- a plea echoed by Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown.
But the campaign has been one of the most bitterly-fought in Britain's political history, with the two ruling parties daily seeking out its rivals' weak points with vicious precision.
The polls suggest their efforts have had little impact. Labour has held a double-digit lead in opinion polls since the election was called on March 17 -- except for one rogue poll.
The latest polls in Friday's newspapers gave Labour leads over the Conservatives of 16 points and 18 points. Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing for a majority in the 659-seat parliament.

Labour tried to bring a softer, more personal, tone to the campaign with an election broadcast on Thursday evening, portraying Blair as a typical family man, who partook in the dirty business of politicking only as a means to an end.

The broadcast was recorded some time ago and Labour was already back on the attack over a report from a children's charity published on Friday which said that poor children in Britain were at risk from malnutrition.
Save the Children said parents on state benefits were unable to afford a balanced diet for their families.
Labour's shadow health secretary Chris Smith called this one of the "appalling consequences" of 18 years of Conservative rule.
Labour, however, which has fought hard to play down its old reputation for high taxes and spending, has made no pledges to raise state benefits.
The Conservatives rejected the charity's claims, saying that surveys over the past 20 years showed that British children were getting taller and healthier.
